content.thinking:
I should be honest that this was actually a latency incident rather than an error-rate one, since errors dropped below baseline while the deploy correlation was confirmed by the rollback. I need to flag that the code-vs-config distinction wasn't diff-verified, keeping confidence around 0.7, and avoid misreporting the brief hold duration as an outage.

I'm noting other assumptions to disclose: the fix attribution to revision 5e07d73 is inferred without an actual deploy diff, recovery was judged from just one metric check ~20 seconds post-rollback, ClientDisconnected errors were treated as noise, and the 13:19 onset was inferred from a metric anchored later at 13:24. The impact window spans roughly six minutes, from 13:19 to 13:25. For the executive summary, I want to avoid naming specific components, so instead of using the service name directly I'll refer to it more generically as the shop's website backend.

assumptions: The deploy at 13:19 is treated as the cause on the strength of timing correlation plus a successful rollback; no code or config diff of revision 5e07d73 was examined, so the specific regressing change is unidentified and 'new code' rather than 'packaged config' remains an inference.

Recovery is taken from a single metric check at 13:25:04, about 20 seconds after the rollback, and the alert was not observed to stay clear over a longer window; a slower-developing recurrence would not have been caught before the incident was closed.
The onset time of 13:19 comes from per-minute metrics anchored at 13:24; minute-granularity data means the true onset could be up to a minute earlier.

The ClientDisconnected errors on the account page appear before, during and after the slowdown at a steady trickle and were judged unrelated background noise rather than a symptom; this was not verified against the deploy.

No evidence was gathered on downstream dependencies, saturation or an external cause; the investigation stopped once the deploy correlation looked strong, so an alternative trigger that happened to coincide with the release was not ruled out.

User impact is characterised as slowness based on latency percentiles alone; no client-side, checkout-completion or traffic-drop data was consulted, so the real-world severity for shoppers is not measured.
The error-rate figures for this window are reported as given and were not independently recomputed; they show no elevation, so the incident is treated as latency-only.
The draft pull request is assumed to address the regression, but its contents were not reviewed here and it does not yet constitute a fix in production.
input.executive_summary: On 25 September 2026 the shop's web service became slow to respond, starting at 13:19 UTC and recovering at 13:25 UTC — about six minutes. Requests during that window were still being served, and the share of failing requests did not rise above its normal level (it was in fact slightly lower than the preceding baseline); the user-visible effect was slowness, with page responses taking seconds rather than fractions of a second, not an outage. The slowdown began in the same minute as a software release to that service. The automated responder picked up the alert at 13:24, investigated the service's metrics, logs and recent production changes, and at 13:24:43 reverted the service to its previous release. Response times were back to normal by 13:25, and the revert was confirmed. A draft pull request proposing a permanent fix was opened shortly afterwards and is not yet merged or reviewed. Note that the alert fired roughly five minutes after the slowdown began, so most of the impact window elapsed before anyone or anything was working the incident.
input.root_cause: A deploy of io-shop revision 5e07d73148d0a704b8fefe5f379bc652bb773655 landed at 13:19:00Z, the exact minute p50/p95/p99 latency stepped up from tens/hundreds of ms to hundreds/thousands of ms and stayed there; with request volume flat, no config-only change recorded, and no recent feature-flag changes, the leading explanation is a latency regression in the newly released code. Rolling the service back off that revision returned latency to baseline, which corroborates the deploy as the trigger, though no deploy diff was inspected to identify the specific change responsible.
